item.title: the happiest man in the kingdom
item.description:
by Kasey Kirchner
//

The king, being a king, got everything he wanted—every dream fulfilled, every hunger sated, every fleeting whim or fancy realized. If he wanted to bathe in rose petals, his devoted servants would brave the thorns. If he wanted to bathe in honey, they would brave the bees. If he wanted to bathe in ox blood, they would brave the beast.

Bathing was the king’s favorite pastime. His extravagant golden tub was large enough to accommodate three people, and he often invited guests to partake in these pleasures with him. He had his favorites, of course, but after a while, he grew bored of their familiar movements, their predictable sounds. It was not uncommon for his excitement to evaporate and for his mood to plummet drastically and without warning. When this happened, he would banish his guests from the bathing room or push himself out of the bath and wander back to bed, dripping and sliding naked through the halls.

item.title: in the scalloped white morning I look for you
item.description:
by Dylan Bourne
//

In the scalloped white morning I look for you, you came
and left before I woke. In my dream: everyone’s face intricate
with grief. Not yours. Your face scraped clean by the
temperature of this rock, by the white stuff floating in the air.

Now my mom half-rigid above the kitchen counter in
green middle day, filling out your death paperwork,
unsure what to be stressed about now without your moans,
your multiplying organs stopped, your shrinking face stopped,
yours fevers cooled, and your worries fully complete and realized:
everything unfinished, only a few videos made, and you left us,
your children, alone with the big stones in the yard, unsure which

is in its right place, which is too heavy to move. But at least
you stopped dreaming of the good-tasting food you could
no longer eat. Mom’s putting you away now. The few videos you
completed were for us, for future key moments in our life. What
did you know about how the days would feel?—summer is still warm,
I see children everywhere, busy parents. But not the same world. In the vacant
street I’ve lined up all your words, your expressions too and the order of your sentences
perfect down the row, but the force that made it all is gone, and no new words come. \\

item.title: the den of gifts
item.description:
by James Cody Phelan
//

A sharp clamor ricocheted through the morning quiet. Gulls sprang from their roosts above drystone homes, squawking in protest. One squabble of birds drifted over to investigate the commotion and spied a human, only just passing through the dying Koumaria shrubs at the northern edge of the village. The creature labored through rocky soil. As it walked, a narrow path grew in its wake. From afar, the gulls studied the figure and the object it carried to carve the path. The item was shiny and noisy and altogether inedible. This upset the gulls. They made their opinion known by defecating globs of pasty waste onto the figure before returning to their roosts in the village.

item.title: white knuckle
item.description:
by Ethan Miller
//

There are those who believe they can manipulate fate. They make promises, offer systems. To manifest the life you want you must focus your mind on the scene you will inhabit once your wildest dreams have been realized. They’ll tell you the quality of your life depends on your resolve to realise your will upon the world.

These teachers position themselves opposite the Original Religions whose profits and priests bemoan this kind of brazen self-assuredness. The old way dictates that one should pray or meditate in a disinterested way. The point is to commune with the divine, not to realise one’s egoic interests. Fate, they tell us, is out of our hands.

item.title: a prince of cups
item.description:
by Gusanito
//

Your Prince of Cups cried of laughter, when you met him, at the old house—the one our friends used to pass down to each other for generations before the landlord sold its memories & the lights that glowed red at night & the cigarette butts fossilized in the crack between the oven and the wall.

¿Could you help me paint the picture?

We were at the round table, near midnight, sharing a joint, Strawberry-Blonde to your right, Auburn to my left. Tell that story again, the one about your high school trip to central America they begged you. Ok ok, yes ¿the one when my teacher had an affair with one of the locals, and she didn’t come back with us? you grinned. ¿What? Your Prince of Cups pinched the bridge of his nose trying to hide his teary eyes, and this made you smile. When you drove him to his St. Louis apartment, he asked you where you’re from and you told him We’re from the same place. He returned the smile: We’ll definitely see each other again, then, and when he saw your car drive away, Your Prince of Cups didn’t see it again until you drove him to the park by Lake Minnetonka. Your Prince of Cups was hurt, in crutches, yet he was the one who helped you hop onto the hammock, by his side, where you read Japanese and Irish love stories aloud. I’m from a family of witches, you told him, and you asked him to pick a card from your tarot deck: the King of Cups. I’m backpacking around Italy for the next two months ¿will you stay here? you asked. Not sure if I’d be able to walk very far, and this made you smile, especially when you were at the base of the Alps & you wrote your prince’s name on the snowy peaks & you borrowed black ink from the nearby cows’ spots to write his name on your journal & you traced his name with your pinky on every beer’s foam & you found him in your deck of cards, every time you played a king & you carved his name onto the metal ring you smithed for him. You gifted Your Prince of Cups that ring the day you drove him back from the Missouri river clad in pink rocks—you were silent mermaids by the waterfall. Your Prince of Cups played with the ring on his index finger; he held your hand under the round table, your friends none the wiser, like in your favorite love stories—the ones with secrets. When you moved to Florence to work at the metal shop, leaving Your Prince of Cups, you didn’t want him to stop loving you, and you told him this in Siena, when he flew to that cobblestone plaza where you shared a spliff—You’re the one for me, you confessed, and he held your hand because I can’t say it back, not confidently, not when we’ve known each other for a few months, not at my age, and not when you live so far. You didn’t smile when you told him Never text me back even though we both wanted him to, you wanted Your Prince of Cups to fight for you, but he listened to you, and you didn’t smile when his plane took off; you didn’t smile on the beaches or behind your welding helmet. You regretted what you asked the Prince of Cups to do, and you finally called him, and you told him the truth—that you still loved him. ¿Why are you telling me this years later? I love someone else, don’t call me again—but you did, again and again: I think about you most days ¿Can we coexist? —and Your Prince of Cups didn’t have the strength to tell you No, because you’ve been singing the same song so many years later, so he gave you a Maybe. Maybe.

item.title: hometown
item.description:
by Annie Sheneman
//

The best advice I got as a twenty-two-year-old came from my friend Esme’s college professor, some guy I’ve never met who teaches theatre at a college I wanted to go to but which did not admit me. The source is less relevant than the advice itself, which was this: you should live at home until it’s holding you back, however long that takes. Esme had kindly offered me this piece of advice in response to my moaning about still living at home with my mother.

item.title: crickets
item.description:
by Lena Castro
//

This is the first time I have seen my father since he got hearing aids. I am home for the holidays, back in my parents’ quiet neighborhood. A respite from the gaudy noise and color of New Orleans, and for once, as we eat dinner around the kitchen table, all three of us converse at a reasonable volume. Hearing aids, miracles, quiet, I thank god.

He held out for over a decade, resistant to such a blatant sign of aging. He’s younger than my mother, but more sensitive about age because his health has never been good. So when we started to notice that he asked constantly for things to be repeated and missed out on large chunks of conversations that took place right in front of him––when he boomed, “Say that again?” across the café table, startling everyone around us and embarrassing both my mother and I, repeatedly, too many times for us not to mention it––he didn’t take our concerns with his normal graceful acquiescence.

item.title: rapture
item.description:
by Jasmine Jones
//

There is an old woman on the train wearing a bikini top and soiled sweatpants and she is crying into her palms, each cry increasing in volume, until they’re all nearly at a scream. Everyone is pretending not to hear. They are in suits and heels and staring at their phones. Or they are like me, talking on the phone, acting oblivious to avoid the shame. “What’s that noise?” my mother asks.
